\chapter{Review --- Six Verbs, One Ending}
\label{ch:spanish-review-yo-go}
\hlchaptermodality{55}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name all six -go verbs and say why the list is closed.}

The club is complete at six - and it was never a club, only six unrelated verbs that converged.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — six verbs, one ending}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-repaso-yo-go}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new in this chapter. Say the \emph{yo} forms of the three verbs you have just met: \emph{poner}, \emph{salir}, \emph{venir}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The set is closed. Six of the commonest verbs in Spanish put an unexpected \textbf{-go} on the \emph{yo} form and nowhere else:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{\emph{yo}} & \textbf{and the rest behaves} \\
\midrule
tener & \textbf{tengo} & normally \\
hacer & \textbf{hago} & normally \\
decir & \textbf{digo} & normally \\
poner & \textbf{pongo} & normally \\
salir & \textbf{salgo} & normally \\
venir & \textbf{vengo} & normally \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six verbs, one oddity, and it lives in exactly one slot. That is a much smaller thing to carry than \textquotedblleft{}six irregular verbs.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Here is what the six chapters could not show you separately.

\textbf{They are not a family.} Nobody decided these six belonged together. They came from different Latin verbs, by different routes, and arrived at the same ending by accident — a \emph{g} that was already in some of the stems, and a sound change that pulled the others into line behind them.

The club is a result, not a rule. Spanish learners are taught \textquotedblleft{}the \emph{-go} verbs\textquotedblright{} as though someone had drawn up a membership list; what actually happened is that six unrelated words drifted into the same shape and then reinforced each other.

That is worth knowing for a practical reason: it tells you the list is \textbf{closed}. A pattern with a cause keeps recruiting. A pattern that is an accident stops.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six \emph{yo} forms in one breath — tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo
  \item for each, the plain infinitive it came from
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Until the six run together as one list.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many verbs take \emph{-go}? (\textbf{Six}.) In how many slots? (\textbf{One} — the \emph{yo} form.) And why does the list not grow? (Because it was never a rule — six unrelated verbs happened to converge.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — putting, leaving, and coming in the singular}

\label{lesson:ES-C13-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve the three bounded singular sets first. Only then widen the memory comparison from three learned \textbf{yo} forms to six.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the complete frame for this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item putting or placing: \textbf{pongo · pones · pone}.
  \item leaving or going out: \textbf{salgo · sales · sale}.
  \item coming: \textbf{vengo · vienes · viene}.
  \item known-word contrast: \textbf{Salgo de Madrid. Vengo de Madrid.}
  \item known singular comparison: \textbf{vengo / tengo · vienes / tienes · viene / tiene}.
\end{itemize}

Now that all three new verbs have been taught, the learned \textbf{yo} comparison can grow to exactly \textbf{tengo · hago · digo · pongo · salgo · vengo}. It remains a retrieval aid, not a rule for predicting any unseen verb.

Plural persons, full boot diagrams, reflexive clothing expressions, house and table nouns, clock times, dinner vocabulary, and other unseen contexts remain outside this checkpoint.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{poner} continues Latin \emph{pōnere}, the placing family of \textbf{position}.
  \item \textbf{salir} continues Latin \emph{salīre}, the leaping family of \textbf{salient}.
  \item \textbf{venir} continues Latin \emph{venīre}, the coming family of \textbf{convene}.
  \item different inherited histories and analogy let the six known \textbf{yo} forms converge on \textbf{-go}; the shared shape does not make a productive prediction rule.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “pongo, pones, pone”
  \item “salgo, sales, sale”
  \item “vengo, vienes, viene”
  \item “tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give all three new singular sets. (\emph{Pongo, pones, pone; salgo, sales, sale; vengo, vienes, viene.}) Which six learned \textbf{yo} forms now share \textbf{-go}? (\emph{Tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo.}) Why is the list a memory aid rather than a prediction rule? (Different histories converged on one shape.) The next chapter may now introduce a new time frame without borrowing any plural form from this chapter.
\end{tcolorbox}
